sections.heading: Claims
sections.text: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly hold side-effecting tools (payments, email, CRM, infrastructure APIs) while reading untrusted content, and common agent-framework defaults conflate two distinct controls: **capability gating** (which tools a model may see and call at all) and **per-call authorization** (whether this concrete invocation, with these argument values, for this principal and session, is allowed). The paper's central claim is that this conflation is a structural default across the frameworks it audited, not an isolated misconfiguration, and that it reproduces the classical confused-deputy failure — the model, having both the ability to name an action and the only voice describing why it should be trusted, ends up supplying its own authorization.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: A public-source architecture review pinned to specific commits/releases: LangChain/LangGraph (commits `00ad96c`/`bdb323e`), LlamaIndex (v0.14.23, commit `520aa4e`), and the Stripe Agent Toolkit (commits `0b4961f`/`f54c9e6`). For each, the audit asks one deterministic question: after the model emits a tool call, is there a fail-closed check over the concrete argument values before the side effect executes? The paper then measures model behavior directly — deployment-tier vs. flagship models' rate of attempting unauthorized calls under naive vs. task-aligned prompt-injection framing — and builds ScopeGate, a five-stage Policy Decision Point/Policy Enforcement Point (scope check → argument-value authorization against operator allowlists → a finite-bounds money ceiling → an idempotency-key requirement for side-effecting calls → default-deny) evaluated against a reproducible LangChain payment proof of concept and a 40-iteration adaptive-attacker budget.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- All three audited frameworks provide capability gating by default; none provides a deterministic, fail-closed, per-call value-authorization gate by default — each is confused-deputy-by-default once an integrator exposes a side-effecting tool.
- Measured attempted-unauthorized-action rate: deployment-tier models averaged 0.603, flagship models 0.189 (~3.2x lower); task-aligned prompt injection raised unauthorized-attempt rates substantially over naive framing in paired comparisons.
- ScopeGate, evaluated against the same attack surface: 0/48 static bypasses, 0/29 unauthorized attempts across a 40-iteration adaptive run, 0/10 benign-request false denies.
- **Authors' own stated limits:** "Containment is not cure" — ScopeGate does not prevent prompt injection, detect poisoned weights, repair model behavior, or guarantee safe natural-language output. The zero-bypass results are explicitly bounded by "the written vectors, attacker, and 40-iteration adaptive budget" and are stated as *not* a universal bypass-impossibility proof. The benchmark is "one author's corpus, one delivery vector, and single-turn scenarios." The audit covers only public-source client defaults, not the internals of any remote/managed service. The paper frames its own contribution narrowly — "the first reproducible cross-framework audit of the default gap," not originality of the per-call-authorization idea itself — and names stateful side channels, DNS rebinding/timing attacks, multi-agent policy poisoning, and multi-turn scope as explicitly out of scope for this pass.
